heading: 1 Introduction
note: One opening paragraph: the river is reachable only by multi-day boat trips, demand has risen, and managers need a schedule that fills the campsites without putting two parties in one site, plus the first definition of optimality. Stored count 9 against one printed paragraph.

heading: 2 Definitions and Numbering (route, orbit, campsites 0..Y+1, trip types 1..26, Chart 1)
note: The working vocabulary laid out as a numbered list: optimal and route (4), orbit (5), campsite numbering downstream (6), trip-type numbering 1 to 26 with Chart 1's oar-powered and motorized rows (7-8), then the symbols A_i for daily travel time (9), n_i for campsites per orbit (10) and m_i for trips in the season (11), where block 11 also carries the 3 Specific formulation heading. Stored count 8 against seven printed units.

heading: 3 Specific Formulation of the Problem
note: One paragraph fixing the geometry and the horizon, Y campsites on a straight segment, 180 days, one campsite a night, then splitting the task into the three parts the paper solves. Stored count 5 against one printed paragraph.

heading: 4 Assumptions
note: Seven numbered assumptions printed as a single block: downstream-only travel, one night per site, under 24 hours between sites, at most 8 hours of boating per day, no two parties in a site, both propulsion types available, and the 150-site test case. Stored count 8 against one printed block, the stored bucket counting the circled items separately.

heading: 5 Part 1: Fixed Dates, Types and Routes (5.1 Method, 5.2 Development)
note: The deterministic model. Section 5.1 justifies fixing routes first, since less freedom gives more room to arrange (14), with Chart 2 summarising it and the trip-type count beginning (15-16). Section 5.2.1 assigns campsites by residue modulo the number of types, 25 after crossing out the two infeasible oar-powered durations (17-18), defines the leader and the forgone loss and writes the fill condition as an inequality chain (19-21), shows Chart 3 for Y = 425 (22), converts given type proportions into orbit sizes through m_i/n_i and the sum of n_i to Y (23-25), builds the seven-site skeleton orbit and its generalisation to every type (26-28), and states the validity condition Y >= 306 (29). Section 5.2.2 handles the small-Y case by putting two types in one orbit with Chart 6 (30-31), Chart 7's first two days and the I j-k notation (32), the resulting carrying capacity 2340 for Y = 150 (33), and 5.2.3 extends the same construction to three types, m types and finally one orbit per propulsion with Chart 8 (34). Stored count 26 against 14 printed units.

heading: 6 Part 2: Fixed Dates and Types, Unrestrained Routes (Greedy)
note: The stochastic greedy model. Section 6.1.1 motivates abandoning fixed routes and states the inclusion-exclusion formula for the collision probability (35-36), defines the auxiliary function Trip(n) and q(x, day) (37), and 6.1.2 states the greedy idea with Chart 9 (38). Section 6.2 keeps 24 trip types under a strict 8-hour day (39), sets up the forward recursion f(T, x, t) over reachable campsites (40-42), turns it into p(T, x, t) and then iterates day by day with Jordan's formula (43-44), and the whole April-to-September schedule is Chart 10 (45-50), including the case where X trips are already booked, which is just the same greedy continued (50). Stored count 42 against eight printed units; the stored bucket counts recursion lines and schedule cells as paragraphs.

heading: 7 Part 3: Fixed Dates, Free Types and Routes
note: The third model gives tourists the choice of type, so the greedy now selects the trip rather than placing a given one (51), with 24 types available and the eight runs reported (52), Charts 11 and 12 giving carrying capacity and the resulting type mix of 2616 oar-powered against 1248 motorized trips (53-54), and the comparison showing the totals barely move from Part 2 (55). Stored count 24 against four printed units.

heading: 8 Testing of the Model: Sensitivity Analysis
note: Three perturbations, each with its own table: the chapter opens on what sensitivity means and why a low-sensitivity model is preferred (56), then all 24 possible first trips are tried and the carrying capacities in Chart 13 move only slightly, which licenses the arbitrary choice (57-58), the 8-hour assumption is relaxed to 7 through 9 hours and Chart 14 shows the response (59-60), and the small-probability threshold is swept over 0.01, 0.025 and 0.05 with Chart 15, a parameter the paper admits cannot be ignored (61-62). Stored count 9 against five printed units.

heading: 9 Evaluation of the Model (9.1 strengths and weaknesses, 9.2 further discussion)
note: The three-part verdict: 9.1.1 lists the strengths part by part, near-complete campsite use, the orbit device that cuts complexity, and applicability to varying Y, then 9.1.2 lists the weaknesses, the unrealistic rigidity of Part 1 and the assumption that all tourists behave alike (63), and 9.2 proposes the practical extensions, including surveys to estimate the real probabilities (64). Stored count 10 against two printed blocks.

heading: 10 Conclusions
note: One conclusion block of 362 words restating the three schedules ordered by flexibility and the managers' choice among them, then closing on the carrying capacities obtained. Stored count 6 counts its sentences.

heading: 12 Letter to the River Managers
note: The one-page letter: the demand pressure, the no-two-parties-in-one-site rule, the three schedules and their capacity figures, and the request that managers pick one for commercial reasons. Stored count 8 counts its sentences.
